decisions.statement: `refuse_personal_access_token` (a route dependency) is on every route that grants or revokes access, creates an account with a typed password, issues the SCIM token, changes single sign-on or `advanced-settings`, and on leaving an organisation; the media-token URL can no longer mark a file confidential.
decisions.rationale: Guard: `test_session_only_routes.py` walks the route table for the whole class. `advanced-settings` was added after the register review because it sets the token lifetime cap and the mail relay (, asked to fix).
decisions.section: Security hardening of the whole product (fixes and guards)

decisions.title: P2, P4
decisions.statement: The scope of a token (organisations, projects) is applied centrally in `accessible_project_ids` (`rbac.restrict_to_session_scope`), and to the organisation list and record, memberships, reviews due and notifications; this amends the earlier "personal endpoints untouched by token scoping" decision ().
decisions.rationale: A redeemed reset link and switching two-factor off revoke the person's tokens; a routine password change does not (, reverses the recorded independence for recovery paths only).
decisions.section: Security hardening of the whole product (fixes and guards)

decisions.title: C1 to C5 (import)
decisions.statement: A person named in a bundle must hold a role in the target organisation, else they are unmatched exactly like an unknown address (also removes the registered-address oracle).
decisions.rationale: Replayed audit events are attributed to the importer with the original actor and time in the detail. An organisation setting `allow_imported_approval_state` (default allowed, ) returns imported records to drafts when off, through the modules' existing `template_reset` hooks run in `keeping_history()` (archived records and authorship kept), and the import audit counts records that arrived beyond draft. Bundles are bounded by entry count, per-entry size, JSON size and compression ratio, and a corrupt entry is a 400. An `image/*` claim must match the bytes (`trusted_content_type`); the email logo is a raster picture only.
decisions.section: Security hardening of the whole product (fixes and guards)

decisions.title: SC1 to SC3, M1, M2, S7, NEW-1
decisions.statement: SCIM `active` is parsed strictly; operations and names are type-checked (400, not 500); lists page in SQL; a platform administrator or deactivated account is not provisioned.
decisions.rationale: The MCP sign-in page mints a personal access token and discards the session token (: the token is scoped to the person's organisations and cannot manage the account). The server instructions say tool text is data. The identity provider client caps responses at 1 MiB, pins the connection to the checked address, caches discovery for 5 minutes and is rate-limited per address.
decisions.section: Security hardening of the whole product (fixes and guards)

decisions.title: G1 to G5, G7
decisions.statement: The demonstration generates its own secrets into an untracked file and refuses placeholders ().
decisions.rationale: The observability profile binds to loopback, has no anonymous access, requires `GRAFANA_ADMIN_PASSWORD`, and Alloy reads containers through a read-only socket proxy. The backend port binds to loopback by default. Keys can be rotated (`APP_SECRET_ENCRYPTION_KEY_PREVIOUS`, `scripts/rotate_secret_key.py`); an unreadable stored secret is counted, logged and checked at start-up. A TOTP code is accepted once and attempts are counted under a row lock. Passwords are 8 to 72 bytes and not on a built-in common list (`services.password_policy`).
decisions.section: Security hardening of the whole product (fixes and guards)

decisions.title: Audit completeness (H2 to H4)
decisions.statement: Comment add, edit, reaction and attachment removal on requirements, change requests and actions are audited (comment id and a body digest, never the body) and kept off the History and Activity pages (`AUDIT_TRAIL_ONLY_ACTIONS`); display name changes, second-factor enrolment, avatar removal, report run output deletion and requirements report downloads are audited; removing a comment attachment now…
decisions.rationale: deletes the stored object. Guard: `test_mutating_routes_audited.py` follows calls from every mutating handler to an audit write and requires a stated reason for each exemption. Audit rows are append-only for the runtime database role (`AUDIT_RUNTIME_ROLE`, `DATABASE_MIGRATION_URL`, `services.audit_protection`); two roles, not a trigger, because the table owner can drop a trigger (). It is off until an operator provisions the role (`docs/deployment.md`).
decisions.section: Security hardening of the whole product (fixes and guards)

decisions.title: S3 to S6, NEW-2, NEW-3, C6
decisions.statement: The front end sends a Content-Security-Policy built at container start from checked values (`script-src 'self'` plus listed origins, `object-src 'none'`, `base-uri`, `form-action`), HSTS behind an HTTPS proxy, a Permissions-Policy and cache headers; API JSON is `no-store`.
decisions.rationale: Actions are pinned to commit SHAs with Dependabot for actions, pip, npm and Docker; publishing is limited to `main` and to a `release` environment; CI gains Bandit (high severity), Semgrep (error severity, Python and front end), Gitleaks over history and tree, and a weekly OWASP ZAP baseline against the test stack, each failing on a high finding with no baseline (). `.gitleaks.toml` lists seven earlier commits whose fake test credentials cannot be rewritten; the sources were changed so the working tree is clean. Findings the first run raised were fixed in code (a weak hash used for a name, a world-writable directory, `text()` with a variable that is now a bound `set_config`); the DDL in disaster recovery keeps a reasoned `nosemgrep`. The converter's memory ceiling, queueing and restart policy were corrected and a person's conversions are rate limited.
decisions.section: Security hardening of the whole product (fixes and guards)

standard.name: SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria (Security and Confidentiality)
standard.description: The 2017 Trust Services Criteria (revised 2022) for Security (CC1 to CC9) and Confidentiality (C1), as assessed in docs/soc2/trust-services-criteria-mapping.md.

criteria.name: Commitment to integrity and ethical values
criteria.control: Company-level code of conduct and ethics policy
criteria.status_note: Organizational action required — Company must adopt and communicate

criteria.name: Board/governance oversight independent of management
criteria.control: Governance structure for the security program
criteria.status_note: Organizational action required

criteria.name: Management establishes structure, authority, and reporting lines
criteria.control: Named information security owner; defined roles for server admin, org admin, engineering, ops
criteria.status_note: Application-level roles exist and are enforced in code (`backend/app/services/rbac.py`); Company-level org chart is a placeholder

criteria.name: Commitment to competence
criteria.control: Hiring, training, and role-appropriate skill requirements
criteria.status_note: Organizational action required

criteria.name: Enforces accountability
criteria.control: Individual accountability for actions is enforced at the system level via per-user audit logging
criteria.evidence: `backend/app/services/audit.py` (`log_event`, records `actor_id` on every mutating action); `LoginEvent` table for authentication events
criteria.status_note: Technically implemented; Company-level performance/accountability process is a placeholder

criteria.name: Obtains/generates quality information to support internal control
criteria.control: System generates structured audit events and login history usable for control monitoring

criteria.name: Internally communicates information necessary for internal control, including objectives and responsibilities
criteria.control: Policies are documented (this package); formal internal communication/training program
criteria.status_note: Documented, but not yet formally communicated/attested by staff — Company action required (the product can record per-person acceptance of published policies once the Company publishes this set there and requires it)

criteria.name: Communicates with external parties (customers, regulators) regarding matters affecting internal control
criteria.control: Customer-facing status/incident communication process; public documentation of the product's security posture
criteria.evidence: [README.md](../../README.md), [enterprise-integration.md](../enterprise-integration.md) describe technical behavior; formal customer notification process
criteria.status_note: Organizational action required

criteria.name: Specifies objectives clearly enough to identify/assess risk
criteria.control: Product requirements and architectural goals are formally documented

criteria.name: Identifies and analyzes risk to objectives, across the entity
criteria.control: Formal, recurring risk assessment process and risk register
criteria.status_note: Process documented as a policy; no risk register or completed assessment exists yet — Company action required

criteria.name: Considers the potential for fraud in assessing risk
criteria.control: Fraud-risk consideration folded into the risk assessment methodology; technical fraud-relevant controls (e.g. self-approval prevention) exist in the product
criteria.evidence: [policies/risk-assessment-policy.md](policies/risk-assessment-policy.md); e.g. a change request's submitter cannot approve their own request (enforced in `backend/app/routers/change_requests.py`, tested in `tests/playwright/tests/e2e-workflows/change-request-approval-separation.spec.ts`)

criteria.name: Identifies and assesses changes that could significantly affect internal control
criteria.control: Architectural/security decisions are logged as they're made, including their risk rationale
criteria.evidence: `docs/decisions.md` (ongoing record of every architectural and security decision, including hardening passes)
criteria.status_note: Practice exists and is evidenced; not yet formalized as a standing process independent of engineering activity

criteria.name: Performs ongoing and/or separate evaluations of whether controls are present and functioning
criteria.control: Automated test suites run on every push/PR and function as continuous control evaluation for application-level controls (RBAC boundaries, auth, workflow guarantees); periodic security review passes
criteria.evidence: `.github/workflows/ci.yml`; backend pytest suite (~95% line coverage, published per run and failing below 93.2%); Playwright E2E suite; `docs/decisions.md`'s hardening-pass sections
criteria.status_note: CI now runs and gates on all of this automatically (was previously manual-only) — see [policies/change-management-and-secure-development-policy.md](policies/change-management-and-secure-development-policy.md). Branch protection requiring the checks to pass before merge is not enforced (the "Main Branch" ruleset is disabled; a GitHub repo setting, not a workflow-file change) — Company action required, checklist in the change-management policy

criteria.name: Evaluates and communicates deficiencies to those responsible for corrective action
criteria.control: Findings from security review passes are documented and remediated, with the fix and rationale recorded
criteria.evidence: `docs/decisions.md` hardening-pass sections; this package's own creation is itself an instance of this (see the round of fixes in the "Massif (v3) hardening pass" section)
criteria.status_note: Demonstrated in practice for engineering-driven reviews; no formal deficiency-tracking system (ticketing, SLA for remediation) exists — Company action required

criteria.name: Selects and develops control activities that mitigate risk to acceptable levels
criteria.control: RBAC, input validation, audit logging, and SSRF/CSRF-class fixes selected in direct response to identified risks

criteria.name: Selects and develops general controls over technology
criteria.control: Environment-variable-driven configuration with fail-fast validation in production; separate dev/test vs. production Compose stacks

criteria.name: Deploys control activities through policies that establish expectations, and procedures that put policies into action
criteria.control: This package
criteria.status_note: Policies drafted; formal deployment (owner sign-off, staff attestation) is a Company action

criteria.name: Implements logical access security software/infrastructure/architecture
criteria.control: JWT-based authentication, bcrypt password hashing, TOTP-based 2FA, per-org OIDC SSO, `token_version`-based mass session revocation, single-use emailed password-reset links and a forced credential reset (command line included); the MCP server (AI-assistant integration — read by default, with opt-in write and, separately, an org-and-project-gated AI-approval capability) reuses this same mechanism rather than a separate credential type, introducing no new access-control surface
criteria.status_note: See [policies/access-control-policy.md](policies/access-control-policy.md)

criteria.name: Registers and authorizes new internal/external users prior to granting access
criteria.control: Org admins provision members and assign roles; SSO users are provisioned on first login gated by an optional required-group check; server admin bootstrap is config-gated; public self-signup (opt-in, domain-gated in "org specified" mode) and admin-initiated project invites (org-opt-in `external_user_policy`) and a server admin's Add user (`POST /system/users`, sharing `services/user_provisioning.py` with Org Admin) are three further, explicitly-authorized provisioning paths — see access-control-policy.md's Provisioning section and its Known Gap on unverified-email trust

criteria.name: Role-based access consistent with least privilege and segregation of duties
criteria.control: Org roles (org_admin, project_creator, member) and project roles (project manager, project administrator, stakeholder, member), independently scoped; server admin explicitly does not inherit organization content access; server-tier roles are explicit route allow-lists, and organisation creation and deletion are held by two independent roles (`SUBSCRIPTION_MANAGER`, `SUBSCRIPTION_REMOVAL_AUTHORITY`) so provisioning and destruction can be segregated; the global search authorises each project and record type (genuine role, module on, `view`) before it queries and omits rather than redacts, so counts disclose nothing
criteria.status_note: A follow-up review found and fixed two endpoints (`deactivate_org_user`, `archive_org_user`) that scoped the caller's role correctly but not the *target* of the action to the same organization — see [policies/access-control-policy.md](policies/access-control-policy.md)

criteria.name: Restricts physical access to facilities and protected information assets
criteria.control: Physical data center security
criteria.evidence: Relies entirely on the hosting/cloud provider — see [system-description.md](system-description.md) §10 (CSOCs)
criteria.status_note: Carve-out to subservice organization — Company must name the provider and reference their report

criteria.name: Discontinues logical/physical access when no longer required
criteria.control: Org admins can deactivate a member (`is_active = False`, immediately rejected on the next REST request and, since the hardening pass, within 60 seconds on an already-open WebSocket connection too); password-change/2FA-disable revoke all outstanding sessions via `token_version`
criteria.status_note: Deactivation and mass session revocation both take effect promptly now; there is still no automated offboarding trigger tied to an HR/identity-lifecycle event — that link is a Company process, not an application feature

criteria.name: Implements controls to protect against threats from outside system boundaries
criteria.control: TLS termination and network exposure are the deployer's responsibility (the app serves plain HTTP internally by design); CORS origin allow-list; SSRF guard on org-configured OIDC endpoints; per-account lockout on the 2FA challenge step after repeated failed codes
criteria.status_note: The first-factor password check has a progressive delay per account and per source address, the second factor a lockout, and the unauthenticated routes shared limits across workers; the client address is the connecting one (`FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS`). The front end sends a Content-Security-Policy and HSTS behind an HTTPS proxy. TLS termination remains the operator's — see [policies/access-control-policy.md](policies/access-control-policy.md) Known Gaps

criteria.name: Restricts the transmission, movement, and removal of information to authorized users/processes
criteria.control: File attachments and reports are served only through authorization-checked endpoints, not directly from storage
criteria.status_note: Authorization-checked endpoints serve files, and the backend reaches the bundled object storage with a single bucket-scoped identity (no other bucket, no bucket listing), and the unauthenticated filer/master APIs are loopback-only; pinned by tests against the live storage service and the compose files. Known limit: the identity can create and delete its own bucket

criteria.name: Prevents or detects and acts upon unauthorized/malicious software
criteria.control: Endpoint/host-level malware protection, dependency vulnerability scanning
criteria.evidence: CI `dependency-scan` job (`pip-audit` for the backend and mcp-server, `npm audit --omit=dev` at high for the frontend and Playwright) and a Trivy scan of every production image before it is pushed (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`); fixable HIGH/CRITICAL findings fail the build
criteria.status_note: Dependency, image, static-analysis (Bandit, Semgrep) and secret (Gitleaks) scanning is automated and gating, and a weekly OWASP ZAP baseline runs against the test stack (`.github/workflows/dynamic-scan.yml`); actions are pinned to commit SHAs. Open: the documentation site's `braces` advisory has no patched release, so that audit is reported, not gating; host-level malware protection and the third-party Compose images are outside this scan — see [policies/change-management-and-secure-development-policy.md](policies/change-management-and-secure-development-policy.md). **Note (modular feature system):** the modular feature system's third-party discovery sources (Python entry points, `EXTRA_MODULES_PATH`) are gated behind `ALLOW_EXTERNAL_MODULES`, default `false` — a deliberate, documented mitigation layered on top of this still-open gap (a plugin-loading mechanism that can auto-import and run third-party code materially raises the stakes of having no automated scanning), not a closure of it; see [policies/vendor-and-subprocessor-management-policy.md](policies/vendor-and-subprocessor-management-policy.md) point 7 and its Known Gaps entry. **Note (module system follow-up, 2026-09-07 — Tier C / Module Federation):** a Tier C frontend module raises these same stakes further still, not merely in the same way as point 7's backend module — it runs with **no sandbox at all** (same origin/DOM/cookies/component tree as the host), where a backend module is at least bounded by the backend process's own authorization checks and Tier B (the modular feature system's *other* dynamic frontend option) is bounded by an iframe sandbox. Gated by the same `ALLOW_EXTERNAL_MODULES` flag, not a second one; see [policies/vendor-and-subprocessor-management-policy.md](policies/vendor-and-subprocessor-management-policy.md) point 8 and its Known Gaps entry 5.

criteria.name: Detects and monitors for configuration changes and vulnerabilities that could introduce risk
criteria.control: Container health checks; optional Prometheus/Loki/Tempo/Grafana Alloy observability stack; disk-usage monitor with alerting
criteria.status_note: Infrastructure/app monitoring exists; dependency and image vulnerability scanning runs in CI — see CC6.8

criteria.name: Monitors system components for anomalies indicative of security events
criteria.control: `/health` and `/metrics` (Prometheus-format) endpoints; structured audit and login-event logging; failed-login events recorded, including 2FA verification attempts and SSO logins (both previously missing, closed in the hardening pass)
criteria.status_note: Data capture is now comprehensive across native, 2FA, and SSO login paths, and audit-event coverage was extended to the mutating endpoints a review found missing it (org branding/report-template/project-settings/component-category/CR-task-vote/custom-field/requirement-link actions); no automated alerting rules/SIEM correlation on top of the captured data exists yet

criteria.name: Evaluates security events to determine whether they represent an incident
criteria.control: Incident classification process
criteria.status_note: Process documented; not yet exercised — Company action required

criteria.name: Responds to identified security incidents
criteria.control: Incident response plan, including concrete technical containment tools (mass session revocation, forced credential reset)

criteria.name: Identifies, develops, and implements activities to recover from identified security incidents
criteria.control: Encrypted, off-site, verified whole-platform backup; restore with guardrails and a credential reset for a possibly exposed copy; automated restore test; schedulers and alerts; recovery runbook
criteria.status_note: Tooling, a weekly restore test (also a CI gate on the tooling itself) and backup alerts exist; the **Company must enable a scheduler and an off-site destination, route the alerts to a person, and exercise a restore on a clean machine** (not yet done, so the recovery time is unmeasured)

criteria.name: Authorizes, designs, develops/acquires, configures, documents, tests, approves, and implements changes to infrastructure, data, software, and procedures
criteria.control: Every change to schema, security-sensitive logic, or architecture is recorded with rationale; automated test suites gate correctness in CI; separate dev/test vs. production Compose stacks prevent test runs from touching production data; production container images are built, scanned and (on `main`) published on every change; a coverage threshold fails the build
criteria.status_note: The CI gate itself now exists and runs automatically; the branch ruleset is Active and CI checks block a merge; **no reviewer approval is required** (0 approvals, accepted: one maintainer) — see [policies/change-management-and-secure-development-policy.md](policies/change-management-and-secure-development-policy.md)

criteria.name: Identifies, selects, and develops risk mitigation activities for risks arising from potential business disruptions
criteria.control: Business continuity / disaster recovery plan
criteria.evidence: Out of scope for this package (Availability TSC not selected — see [README.md](README.md) §Scope); the technical disaster-recovery runbook ([disaster-recovery.md](../disaster-recovery.md): RPO, key custody, restore modes, restore test) exists as a foundation
criteria.status_note: Out of scope by decision, but flagged: any future Availability-scoped engagement still needs a formal business-continuity plan (roles, communication, recovery time objective, an exercised game day), which does not exist

criteria.name: Manages risks associated with vendors and business partners
criteria.control: Vendor identification, due diligence, and ongoing monitoring
criteria.status_note: Subservice organizations identified structurally; no due-diligence records or subprocessor list exist yet — Company action required

criteria.name: Identifies and maintains confidential information to meet the entity's objectives
criteria.control: Data classification scheme; multi-tenant isolation enforced at the RBAC/query layer; secrets sourced from environment configuration, never hardcoded; genuine secret columns (`oidc_client_secret`, `smtp_password`, `totp_secret`) encrypted at the application layer; personal-data columns of record exports and imports excluded unless the organisation policy and the person's `export_personal_data` permission both allow them
criteria.evidence: [policies/data-classification-and-confidentiality-policy.md](policies/data-classification-and-confidentiality-policy.md); `backend/app/services/rbac.py`; `backend/app/models/encrypted_type.py`; `backend/app/services/record_policy.py` (personal data in record exports and imports); [system-description.md](system-description.md) §7
criteria.status_note: The previously-known plaintext-secret gap is resolved; see [policies/encryption-and-key-management-policy.md](policies/encryption-and-key-management-policy.md)

policies.title: Change Management and Secure Development Policy
System Operations, Monitoring, and Logging Policy

gaps.title: The backup credential on the bundled object store can write
gaps.statement: The backup only reads the object store, but SeaweedFS 3.97 refuses an identity every operation unless it holds `Write` on the bucket, so the bundled `backup` service uses the application's own S3 identity (the `restore` service must, because it writes objects back). A defect in the backup tool could therefore modify the store; the compensating control is a test that fails if a backup run makes any call other than list and get. With an external S3 service a genuinely read-only identity (`s3:ListBucket`, `s3:GetObject`) is configured through `BACKUP_STORAGE_ACCESS_KEY` and `BACKUP_STORAGE_SECRET_KEY`; that path is unit-tested but has not been exercised against a read-only-capable store. The `backup` and `restore` services hold database credentials, have no listener or Docker socket and run with all capabilities dropped; authority to run a restore or a credential reset comes from shell access to the deployment, and each use is audited (`cli:<os user>`). See docs/disaster-recovery.md.

gaps.title: The demonstration command publishes a fixed password
gaps.statement: `scripts/demo_setup.py --demo` (a demonstration deployment only) creates three accounts with the documented password `DemoDemo123!` and publishes the sign-in details in a server-wide, non-dismissible message on the login pages; `--rotate-passwords` replaces it with a random password per run. This is a deliberate exception (a demonstration holds sample data only): the command requires `--demo`, a mail catcher as the SMTP relay, and refuses a database holding any organisation it did not create unless the database name is typed; it refuses to publish if a listed account is a server administrator or belongs to another organisation, and never sends the message as a notification or logs the password. It does not weaken the password rule, two-factor or rate limits. See `docs/decisions.md`.

gaps.title: Accepted exception: no reviewer approval before merge (Decided by: User, 2026-10-23)
gaps.statement: The "Main Branch" ruleset is Active, requires a pull request and the five CI jobs with strict up-to-date merging, so a failing job blocks a merge. It requires 0 approvals because the project has one maintainer and nobody else can approve; GitHub does not let an author approve their own pull request, so 1 approval would block every merge. There is therefore no segregation of duties between author and merger; the compensating controls are the CI gates, the decisions log and the security-review pass in this policy. Close it by raising the count to 1 when a second reviewer exists, then update this section and the control matrix (CC8.1).

gaps.title: Pre-release migration convention
gaps.statement: during initial development, schema changes are folded into the single baseline migration rather than issued as incremental Alembic revisions (documented in `docs/decisions.md`). This is appropriate before a first production release but must stop once real production data exists — every schema change after that point needs its own forward migration, since the baseline-squash convention would otherwise require a destructive `down -v` against live data.

gaps.title: No formal reconciliation against actual customer contract language
gaps.statement: has been performed — the classification scheme reflects the system's technical behavior, not a review of specific promises made to customers.

gaps.title: No general hard-deletion capability exists for individual user accounts or for content within a still-active organization
gaps.statement: (a single project, a single user's data) — only deactivation/archival at that granularity. *Narrowed 2026-10-05:* a Stakeholder record (a named person's contact information) can now be permanently erased on its own (see Implementation above); *narrowed again 2026-10-13* to include a single Engagement record (a contact log entry and everything attached to it); the gap stays open for user accounts, projects, and every other record type. Organizations themselves are no longer part of this gap: `DELETE /orgs/{id}` performs genuine hard deletion of the org and everything it owns, including object-storage files (see Implementation above and `docs/decisions.md`). If the Company makes a contractual or regulatory commitment to erase an individual user's or project's data without deleting the whole organization, that remains a real functional gap needing the same treatment (cascading row removal + storage-file removal) at a finer grain.

gaps.title: Erased data persists in backups until retention expires
gaps.statement: (see Implementation). Shortening the retention is the only lever; there is no per-record purge from existing sets, and none is planned, because rewriting immutable encrypted snapshots would defeat their integrity guarantees. The Company must reflect the retention window in what it tells customers about erasure.

gaps.title: Stored report output reaches backups
gaps.statement: A background report's file lives in the object store, so the object mirror and every backup set taken while it exists contain it (encrypted, like the rest of the mirror). Deleting it on expiry, on request (the delete route; the product no longer shows a button for it) or with the organisation removes it from production and from the mirror at the next run, not from older backup sets; the short retention (7 days by default) bounds how much report content a backup can hold. *Closed in the same change:* custom report run records are now expired by the platform retention (`REPORT_RUN_RECORD_RETENTION_DAYS`) and stored output expires on the organisation's setting.

gaps.title: No retention schedule has been formally adopted
gaps.statement: the table above is a starting recommendation, not a decision.

gaps.title: Organization.smtp_password
gaps.statement: was found, during this hardening pass, to be the same risk class as the two gaps above but not yet disclosed anywhere — it is now also `EncryptedString`, closed in the same change rather than left as a separate future gap.

gaps.title: No key rotation process is documented
gaps.statement: for `JWT_SECRET`, `APP_SECRET_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, or subprocessor credentials. Recommendation: define a rotation cadence and a process for rotating each without invalidating every session/re-encrypting every secret abruptly (e.g. dual-key verification during a transition window; for `APP_SECRET_ENCRYPTION_KEY` specifically, a rotation would need to decrypt-under-old-key/re-encrypt-under-new-key for every affected row, since `EncryptedString` as implemented uses a single active key, not key-versioned ciphertext).

gaps.title: Infrastructure-level encryption at rest has not been verified
gaps.statement: for the remaining data categories (requirement/change-request content, file attachments, audit logs) — it depends entirely on deployment configuration outside this repository.

gaps.title: No automated alerting exists to trigger this plan
gaps.statement: detection today depends on someone looking at logs/metrics or a report coming in, not a system paging someone. See system-operations-monitoring-and-logging-policy.md Known Gaps.

gaps.title: No incident has been formally logged or exercised under this plan yet
gaps.statement: it is untested in practice. A tabletop exercise is strongly recommended before relying on this plan under real conditions.

gaps.title: Audit log integrity
gaps.statement: `audit_events` rows are ordinary database rows, not tamper-evident (no hashing/append-only/WORM storage). An attacker with direct database write access could alter or delete audit history. This is an acceptable residual risk for most deployments (database access is already a high-privilege boundary) but should be stated explicitly rather than assumed away, and considered if the Company's threat model includes insider risk from those with direct database access.

gaps.title: No formal governance structure, named owner, or staff communication/attestation process exists yet — this is the primary Company action item this policy package surfaces
gaps.statement: No formal governance structure, named owner, or staff communication/attestation process exists yet — this is the primary Company action item this policy package surfaces. See trust-services-criteria-mapping.md CC1/CC2 rows.

gaps.title: The size ceilings are in the application only; no proxy limit is shipped
gaps.statement: Every request body is capped at `MAX_REQUEST_BODY_BYTES` (52 MB, `body_limit.BodySizeLimitMiddleware`, 413 before the body is read), a single uploaded file at `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` (50 MB, `services.files.upload_file`), and bundle and spreadsheet imports at 200 MB (`services.bundle_common`). There is still no per-organisation storage quota, no request-rate limit on uploads and no limit at the reverse proxy; a deployment should set `client_max_body_size` (or equivalent) to the same order of magnitude. Recommendation: a per-organisation storage quota.

gaps.title: Backups run only when the operator turns a scheduler on
gaps.statement: the schedulers and a weekly restore test ship, but none is enabled by default (a deployment that enables none is flagged by the `ReqTrackBackupMetricsMissing` alert only if the observability stack is also running). The Company must enable one, set an off-site destination and record the schedule. A restore on a clean machine from the off-site copy alone (a game day) has not yet been exercised, so the recovery time is unmeasured.

gaps.title: Alert rules exist for backups only, and nothing routes them to a person
gaps.statement: the backup and restore-test alerts ship, but the bundled Prometheus has no Alertmanager, and there are no rules on the application's own metrics. Grafana provisions only a Prometheus data source and a resource-usage dashboard, with no alert rules on them. Alert routing and an escalation path are a Company configuration task.

gaps.title: No distributed tracing is emitted yet
gaps.statement: the Tempo/Alloy pipeline is deployed and ready to receive traces, but the backend does not instrument requests with OpenTelemetry spans.

gaps.title: Grafana's bundled configuration enables anonymous viewer access
gaps.statement: , appropriate only for local development — a production deployment of the observability stack must put Grafana behind the same authentication/reverse-proxy layer as the rest of the system (documented in deployment.md, but worth restating here as a control requirement, not just a deployment tip).

gaps.title: cAdvisor (observability profile only) mounts the Docker socket read-only and /sys, and holds the SYSLOG capability
gaps.statement: to read OOM kills from the kernel log. A read-only socket mount still exposes the full Docker API to the process; Grafana Alloy no longer holds the socket and reads container metadata and logs through a read-only socket proxy that allows container calls only; the compensating controls are that it lives only in the opt-in profile, publishes no port, is not privileged and has no write mounts (pinned by `backend/tests/test_resource_dashboard.py`). It lists every container the daemon runs, not only this stack's.

gaps.title: No maintained subprocessor list exists yet
gaps.statement: the categories are known structurally, but the actual named vendors, their access scope, and their own compliance posture have not been documented. This is the primary action item.

gaps.title: No formal due-diligence records exist
gaps.statement: for any vendor currently in use.

gaps.title: Credential scoping for subprocessors other than the bundled object storage service is unverified
gaps.statement: The bundled service is scoped (see Implementation above); for SMTP and cloud IAM credentials, and for an external S3 provider, the deployer must scope them in that provider's own IAM and the application cannot check that they did.

gaps.title: No automated vetting of installed third-party modules exists yet
gaps.statement: , beyond policy point 7 above (the `ALLOW_EXTERNAL_MODULES` opt-in gate and the manual due-diligence recommendation) — there is no dependency/vulnerability scanning of a module package before or after it's installed. This is the same underlying gap trust-services-criteria-mapping.md's CC6.8 row already documents ("no automated dependency/container vulnerability scanning exists"), which a plugin-loading mechanism that can run third-party code materially raises the stakes of — the off-by-default gate is a deliberate mitigation layered on top of that still-open gap, not a closure of it.

gaps.title: No sandboxing at all exists for a Tier C frontend module
gaps.statement: (point 8 above) — beyond the shared `ALLOW_EXTERNAL_MODULES` opt-in gate and the deployment operator's own manual review, there is no runtime isolation standing between a loaded Tier C module's code and the rest of the running application (no iframe, no separate origin, no restricted permissions of any kind). This is a materially larger gap than point 4 above, not the same gap restated: point 4 is about the *absence of automated vetting before/after* installing code that then runs behind further architectural boundaries (a backend process boundary for point 7's module, an iframe sandbox for Tier B); this point is about the *absence of any such boundary at all* for a Tier C module once it loads. Mitigating this with a real sandbox (e.g. running Tier C code in a separate worker/origin with a narrow message-passing contract, the same shape as Tier B's own iframe/Host-UI-Bridge design) was considered and explicitly rejected for Tier C specifically, since native, unmediated component-tree/shared-React-instance reuse — which a sandbox boundary would preclude — was the entire stated reason to choose Tier C over Tier B for a given third-party module in the first place; an operator wanting a sandboxed third-party module should choose Tier B instead.

gaps.title: Microsoft Clarity is an optional, demonstration-only subprocessor
gaps.statement: When an operator sets `DEMO_CLARITY_PROJECT_ID` (`scripts/demo.sh --clarity`), the frontend loads Microsoft Clarity's script from `clarity.ms`, which records sessions in the browser and sends them to Microsoft. It is off unless set, the identifier is validated before it is placed in a script address, and masking is configured in the operator's own Clarity project (Strict is recommended). A production deployment must not set it: Clarity would receive screen content that may be Confidential or Restricted. No due-diligence record exists for the vendor, which is the same gap as item 2.

gaps.title: ghcr.io is the demonstration's image source, trusted without a signature check
gaps.statement: `scripts/demo.sh --pull` (daily, from a host timer) runs whatever this repository's CI published under the `latest` tag (or the pinned `IMAGE_TAG`) on ghcr.io; the pushing job runs only from a passing `main` build. The packages are public and carry a provenance attestation, but they are not signed and `--pull` verifies neither, so the demonstration trusts the registry's content for this repository's name. Third-party images are pinned versions. Accepted for a demonstration that holds sample data only (**Decided by: Agent**, to veto); signing the images and verifying before recreating closes it.

principles.name: Layered separation of concerns
principles.statement: The solution separates the user interface, application services, persistence, and operational concerns. This reduces coupling and allows each layer to evolve independently.

principles.name: Domain-driven backend modules
principles.statement: The backend is structured around business domains such as organizations, projects, requirements, change requests, reviews, audit history, and reporting. This makes the system easier to maintain and extend.

principles.name: Container-first deployment
principles.statement: The application is designed to run in containers from the start. Docker Compose provides a development and test environment, and the same model can be used for lightweight production deployments. The demonstration stack adds a Caddy reverse proxy in front of the same application images. It terminates TLS, redirects HTTP to HTTPS, serves the application on one origin and is the only published listener ([demo.md](demo.md#https)). Production keeps the operator's own proxy. The demonstration can also refresh its images on the daily reset: a host timer runs `scripts/demo.sh --pull --reset`, which pulls the published images, recreates only the services whose image changed and then resets and seeds with the new code (no container is given the Docker socket). ```mermaid flowchart LR T["Host timer"] --> S["demo.sh --pull --reset"] S --> R["ghcr.io: pull"] S --> C["Recreate changed services"] C --> D["demo_setup.py reset and seed"] ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR B["Browser"] -->|HTTPS| C["Caddy (demonstration only)"] C -->|"/api/*"| BE["Backend"] C -->|"/"| F["Frontend"] C -->|"mcp host"| M["MCP server"] BE --> DB[("PostgreSQL")] ```

principles.name: Secure-by-default design
principles.statement: Authentication, authorization, audit logging, and data sanitization are treated as first-class platform concerns rather than afterthoughts.
